name: Ozone therapy for gums

card.summary: Ozone applied to the mouth as a gum-disease treatment; ozone therapy broadly is unproven and the FDA says ozone has no demonstrated safe medical use.
card.aka: Dental ozone, ozonated oil for gums
card.note: FDA says ozone is a toxic gas with no demonstrated safe medical use.

quick.overview:
Ozone therapy for gums means using ozone gas, ozonated water or ozonated oil in the mouth to try to treat gum disease. It is the dental branch of a wider alternative medicine practice.

Public summaries of ozone therapy describe evidence for most uses as limited, and no gum-specific trial results were found in the sources reviewed here.
quick.mechanism: Ozone is a strong oxidising gas that can kill microbes in the laboratory; proponents extend this to bacteria in the gums.
quick.risks: The FDA has stated that ozone is toxic and has no demonstrated safe medical use. Serious harms are documented mainly for injected or systemic ozone, not dental use specifically.

lead: Ozone therapy for gums is the use of ozone (O3) in the mouth, as a gas, ozonated water or ozonated oil, to treat gum disease and related dental problems. It is a dental application of ozone therapy, a practice that introduces ozone into the body as an alternative medicine treatment.[1] People use it hoping to reduce oral bacteria, calm inflamed gums and keep a healthy gum line around the teeth.

Proponents describe ozone as a germ-killing agent that can lower bacterial load and support gum healing. A 2026 meta-analysis of randomized trials found that ozonated gels and oils were linked to favorable periodontal outcomes, mainly as adjuncts to subgingival instrumentation, with no major adverse effects reported and with short follow-up limiting the evidence.[2] A 2026 umbrella review found mixed results for chronic periodontitis, with one meta-analysis showing no adjunctive benefit and a newer one reporting gains in probing depth and gingival index.[2]
Regulators take a different position on ozone generally: the US FDA has stated that ozone is a toxic gas with no known useful medical application in specific, adjunctive or preventive therapy.[1]

chain: Ozone gas, water or oil applied to gums
Antimicrobial action on oral bacteria (as proposed)
Healthier gum line around the teeth
angle.text: People and some dental practitioners use ozone to reduce bacteria around the gums as an add-on to professional cleaning. The outcomes studied are gum scores such as probing depth and bleeding rather than appearance.

paras: Ozone was first used in healthcare in 1856, about 16 years after its discovery, to disinfect operating rooms and instruments, and during World War I it was tested on wounds, where it was reported to damage both bacteria and human tissue so that antiseptic irrigation was preferred.[1] Wikipedia lists proposed uses of ozone therapy ranging from osteoarthritis and herniated discs to chronic wounds, and says evidence for many is limited.[1]

The FDA has prohibited medical uses of ozone lacking proof of safety and effectiveness, and has prosecuted sellers of ozone therapy as a cure since 1991.[1] Brazil legalized ozone as a complementary therapy in August 2023, while Malaysia banned it in 2017.[1] Reported serious harms come from systemic routes, including pulmonary edema and gas embolism, rather than dental application specifically.[1]

A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis in Clinical and Experimental Dental Research of randomized trials of ozonated gels and oils in periodontitis found favorable periodontal outcomes, mainly as adjuncts to subgingival instrumentation, with no major adverse effects reported and limited by short follow-up and heterogeneity.[2] A 2026 umbrella review of ozone therapy reported mixed evidence for chronic periodontitis and concluded routine clinical use was not yet justified.[2] A 2025 meta-analysis in Frontiers in Oral Health found that olive oil and ozonated olive oil improved bleeding on probing in periodontitis at 8 to 12 weeks without changes in probing depth or attachment level, and reduced plaque, gingival and bleeding indices in gingivitis in the short term.[2]

timeline.event: Ozone first used in healthcare to disinfect operating rooms and instruments.[1]
FDA begins prosecuting sellers of ozone therapy as a cure.[1]
Meta-analysis of ozonated gels and oils in periodontitis published.[2]
